tone_statements.citation: Blench, Roger, John Muniru & Luther Hon. 2015/2016. Gyem: an endangered East Kainji language of Northern Nigeria. Draft ms., 15 pp. -- the original PDF (academia.edu 16619179 / rogerblench.info), to replace the HTML-embedded text and recover pp. 14-15 datasheets.
tone_statements.quote: Gyem has two level tones and rising and [rare] falling tones. Shimizu (1982a) records downstep but there is no evidence for this in the recordings. Some of the glide tones arise from long vowels and diphthongs, but others occur on single vowels. Tones are marked as follows; HIGH acute accent above the syllable ´ LOW grave accent over the syllable ` RISING hachek over the syllable ˇ Examples are; wing òbèkè seven súndárè who? mǎy Almost all words begin with a low tone. Exceptions are pronouns and some numerals.
tone_statements.locator: Sec. 3.3 'Tones', p. 5 (plus Sec. 4 'Noun morphology', p. 9, last paragraph before 5. Conclusion: 'Unlike many languages in this area, tone in nouns is remarkably static. Prefixes are always low and stem tone is identical in singular and plural.')
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 level (H, L) + rising and [rare] falling contours; no downstep

tone.says: Sec. 3.3: two level tones (H, L) plus a rising and a rare falling glide; Shimizu (1982a) recorded downstep but the authors find no evidence for it in their recordings; some glides come from long vowels/diphthongs, others sit on single vowels; almost all words begin with a low tone (exceptions: pronouns, some numerals). Sec. 4: 'Unlike many languages in this area, tone in nouns is remarkably static. Prefixes are always low and stem tone is identical in singular and plural.' No mention of stress…
